endorsements.title: CHAI AI governance frameworks (playbooks)
endorsements.quote: Agent-specific guardrails (for autonomous solutions): Develop action allow-lists, environment isolation, dryrun modes for high-impact actions, and per-action audit logs.

endorsements.title: Beyond Chatbots: Moving Toward Multistep Modular AI Agents in Medical Education
endorsements.quote: All drafts are automatically logged with source, model, prompt card, and a summary that enables traceability.

endorsements.title: Drone-delivered automated external defibrillators in prehospital emergency care: implementation evidence, bottlenecks, and conceptual integration with artificial intelligence and next-generation communications
endorsements.quote: Additional safeguards should include real-time system-health checks, predefined mission-abort thresholds, safe-landing procedures, adequate battery reserve, manual override, cybersecurity protection, and auditable event logs.

evidence.title: HAARF: Healthcare AI Agents Regulatory Framework - A Comprehensive Security Verification Standard for Autonomous AI Systems in Clinical Environments
evidence.outcome: Unauthorized tool execution by agent with vs without deterministic middleware enforcement in adversarial scenarios
evidence.effect: Baseline agent executed unauthorized tools in 56–60% of adversarial trials; with HAARF middleware unauthorized-tool success rate fell to 0% (95% Wilson CI [0.00, 0.07]); replicated across two models.
evidence.quote: In baseline conditions, the agent model executes unauthorized tools in 56–60% of adversarial trials.

evidence.title: Optimizing genomics-aware clinical agents in precision oncology
evidence.outcome: Rubric and embedding-recall performance of constrained curated-tool agent versus unconstrained broad-tool agents
evidence.effect: Workflow-orchestrated agent with 20 curated tools outperformed all alternatives on five rubric axes including safety; embedding recall 0.877 (MedCPT) and 0.803 (Arctic), p<0.05 versus all full-sample arms.
evidence.quote: The workflow-orchestrated agent outperforms all alternatives on five rubric axes (guideline concordance, correctness, patient centricity, reasoning transparency, and safety) and achieves the highest embedding recall under both a biomedical (MedCPT, R = 0.877) and general-purpose (Snowflake Arctic, R = 0.803) model, significantly exceeding all full-sample arms (p < 0.05, Bonferroni-corrected).

commentary.bottom_line: Two offline simulation studies suggest that restricting an agent to permitted tools may sharply reduce unauthorized actions, with one reporting a drop from 56–60% of adversarial trials to 0%. No study tested isolated execution environments, dry-run previews, or per-action audit logs, and none measured effects in live clinical use.

perspectives.view: Both studies are level 4 simulations with no patient outcomes, so directness is low. Each tests only the allow-list or curated-tool component of the bundle. The 0% rate (95% CI 0.00 to 0.07) rests on 50 trials per condition, which limits precision. Consistency in direction is favorable, but certainty remains very low.

Deterministic middleware blocked every unauthorized tool call in adversarial trials across two models, which suggests enforcement outside the model may catch errors that prompting alone misses. A curated 20-tool agent also scored higher on a safety rubric. Neither study shows whether audit logs or dry-run previews help staff detect or reverse harmful actions.

The curated-tool agent answered 375 clinician-authored questions across 41 cases with embedding recall of 0.877 and 0.803, outperforming broader-tool agents (p<0.05). This suggests tool restriction may not cost answer quality. Both tests ran offline, so workflow burden, latency, and fidelity of the controls in production systems are unmeasured.

Neither study reported testing with Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. One study did not report its setting, and the other drew on international adversarial scenarios. The evidence therefore cannot show whether these controls perform equally across patient groups.

commentary.research_gap: No study has tested isolated execution environments, dry-run previews of high-impact actions, or per-action audit logs, and no study has evaluated any part of the bundle in live clinical deployment. Prospective studies should measure unauthorized-action rates, time to detect and trace errors from logs, staff burden of reviewing previews, and patient-level harms.
commentary.underserved_note: Neither test reported including Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations, so health systems serving these groups have no direct evidence that the controls work as intended for their patients.
